summary:
Huancavelica stands under Peru's national framework. The region has no recorded trans-specific law, ordinance, enforcement pattern or incident of its own, so what a trans visitor to Huancavelica faces is the national position: no criminalisation of trans identity, but statutory restriction of access to public facilities, no hate-crime protection, and rising recorded violence.

Peru's Congress has legislated directly against trans people's use of public facilities. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents mandates that restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Hate-crime protection for LGBT people was stripped from the Penal Code in 2017, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

The restriction reached committee stage in February 2025. Infobae Perú reported on 20 February that the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. Exceptions are narrow: custody, situations requiring medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The text also bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport.

LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory and warned that restroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity checks, noting there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the text and exempted it from a second vote. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, holds that article 5, barring entry to any public sanitary service that does not correspond to 'biological sex', violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The institute finds the provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by implicitly framing them as harassment risks, resting on a stigmatising stereotype that UN reporting contradicts, since trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

Peru's constitutional baseline points the other way. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Recorded violence is rising and under-counted. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases across Peru over 2020-2023. Trans women are more than half the homicide victims at 30, against 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, of whom 12 were trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 complaints lodged in 2020 alone. Report co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stresses that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

One 2023 killing illustrates the pattern: in February 2023 a gang abducted trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and killed her in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme.

Enforcement of the bathroom restriction reaches private life as well as public facilities. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.
tangentialFactors:
IDEHPUCP's legal analysis records dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu during debate of the bathroom provisions, evidence of the tone of official discourse a visitor may encounter in national media coverage.

The 2017 repeal of LGBT hate-crime coverage was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures, indicating the organised political base behind the exclusion rather than an incidental drafting outcome.

Two protective developments are on record and cut against the restrictive trend. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained alongside facilities access. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Comparatively, the bathroom restriction places Peru alongside jurisdictions that legislate facility access by birth sex rather than by recognised gender identity, while its hate-crime law sits with Paraguay and Guyana as the South American states lacking LGBT coverage.
localsOnly:
Residents of Huancavelica have no regional instrument creating trans-specific protections or offences; the governing rules are national, and the region's record contains no ordinance, enforcement pattern or documented incident of its own.

National hate-crime law offers LGBT people no anti-discrimination coverage after the 2017 repeal, so residents cannot rely on Penal Code hate-crime provisions for conduct motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity.

Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed nationwide, trans women most affected, and a 2024 report found hate crimes rising with trans women the most affected group; its co-author Gianna Camacho notes the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reached through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Healthcare settings changed in June 2024, when health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official guidance, and a July 2025 Lima constitutional court struck down an anti-equality decree after an activist challenge.

Residents face the April 2025 law's censorship provisions directly: article 4 restricts media and advertising content, and the minimum obscenity sentence rose from three to four years.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Huancavelica-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding appears in the inventory for any of the three sources; the region's profile rests entirely on the national framework, and whether the bathroom restriction has been applied by security staff in Huancavelica is unresolved and not sourced.

The inventory does not state the promulgation or entry-into-force date of the fused text approved on 2 April 2025, nor whether bills 6506 and 8457 were subsequently enacted as law; the April 2025 Law on Sexual Integrity is separately sourced as mandating 'biological sex' for restroom entry. The relationship between the two instruments is not resolved here.

The scope of the July 2025 constitutional court ruling against an anti-equality decree beyond the issuing court's territorial competence is not sourced, as is whether any appeal followed.

The dismissal of the trans woman's gym complaint by a consumer-protection body is a single recorded decision; whether it establishes a general enforcement posture is unresolved.

Homicide and violation totals for 2020-2023 are drawn from one observatory's registry, and the report's own co-author describes the figures as a sub-registry, so national totals should be read as documented minimums rather than complete counts.
